title: Dress and its Social Functions

paragraphs.text: Throughout history, clothing has served many social purposes. One of the most fundamental aspects of dress in most societies is the custom that the dress of men and women should be different. These differences reflect culturally-determined views of the social roles appropriate to each gender. What is considered appropriate may differ markedly from one place to another. For many centuries in Western Europe, for example, trousers were generally designated as male dress. Clothing may also serve to mark age associated changes. Thus throughout the 19th century, younger girls in Western Europe wore shorter skirts than their adolescent sisters. What a person wears may also convey other information about the wearer, as when a wedding ring worn on a specific finger signifies that he or she is in a marital relationship. Similarly, it was once customary in Europe for married women to cover their hair, while young unmarried women were permitted to go without head covering.

A uniform or a particular style of dress may also be related to the wearer's occupation. However, dress designating occupational status is not limited to a uniform. Thus for many years, particularly during the 1950s and 1960s, men employed by certain companies in the United States were required to wear white shirts with ties to work. Colored shirts were not permitted.

In some cultures, certain types of clothing have been restricted to persons of a particular social rank. These restrictions were sometimes codified into what were known as 'Sumptuary Laws', which restricted the use of luxury goods such as clothing and household furnishings. Thus during the 14th century in England servants were not permitted to wear any article of gold or silver, embroidery or silver. Nowadays, dress is still used to identify an individual as belonging to a particular social group. A uniform or insignia may be adopted formally by that group and kept for its members alone. At other times, group identification is demonstrated by an informal kind of uniform, such as those adopted by adolescents who belong to the same clique.

Dress, therefore, discloses the social stratification of society, revealing whether it has rigid delineations of social and economic class or is a relatively classless society. For example, the political leaders in the African Ashanti tribe wore distinctive dress marking their special social position. No subject was allowed to wear the same fabric pattern as the king. The nature of this political structure — an absolute monarchy — was mirrored in the attitude to clothing. Other aspects of social organization may be manifest in dress. The garments worn by those leading a religious service may or may not distinguish them from the worshippers, again reflecting the way that religion is seen by members of that community.

As well as differentiating between social groups, clothing also serves other purposes. Sociologists speak of rites of passage, marking the passage of the individual from one status to another. Specific costumes exist in modern American society that are considered appropriate for graduations, weddings, baptisms, and burials. Special clothing may also be involved in ceremonies which serve to strengthen the community, as when the inhabitants of a town dress in historic costume to celebrate the anniversary of the founding of the town. Designated forms of dress are frequently an important part of the ceremonies associated with such rites. Clothing is also a means of enhancing the attractiveness of individuals. This may be achieved by focusing attention on a particular part of the body, or by clothes which make the wearer appear affluent and successful.

The historical context is also important. Fashion may be affected when governments pass legislation to regulate clothing-related industries, or by the desire of individuals or groups to imitate clothing worn by charismatic political leaders. Another related theme is political conflict. Access to the raw materials needed for clothing may be reduced by war, or this may produce the opposite effect and through the introduction of new materials and ideas, result in the expansion of alternative types of dress. The disappearance of nylon from the consumer market in the 1940s when it was diverted for use in military equipment, or the widespread adoption of the trench coat, formerly only an item of military dress, in the early 1920s, are examples of this.

Economic events and trade may also be significant. These may be the result of government policies or shaped by unexpected occurrences such as the discovery of valuable natural resources. Such themes were evident when the economic depression of the 1930s was accompanied by a shift from ornate, decorative clothing to more subdued styles, or when the opening of the silk trade with China by the Romans at the end of the 1st century B.C. made this fabric available to upper-class Romans.

The production of textiles and clothing is closely related to the advance of technology. One dramatic example from the 19th and early 20th centuries was the increase in the mass production of clothing in the United States, which made possible the modern fashion industry. Technology may also have an impact on areas such as transportation, communications or production of consumer goods, each of which in turn may affect dress. Examples range from the invention of the sewing machine, without which mass production would have been impossible, to the development of the bicycle, which encouraged the wearing of shorter skirts by women.

questions.prompt: In England, restrictions on the dress of servants were once enforced by law.
The use of clothing as a sign of group identity is more common among male adolescents than among females.
The Ashanti tribe is referred to as an example of a classless society.
A wedding is an example of an event celebrated to strengthen the community.
Clothes designed for military use may later become popular.
An economic depression may be caused by a lack of natural resources.
The sewing machine was an essential factor in the development of the modern fashion industry.

subtitle: How does fashion emerge from and interact with the society that produces it?
